title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 10
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (a memoir-style narrative, a social science passage on language and schooling with a data table, a humanities passage on the mashrabiya and a natural science passage on ocean chemistry), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**: **36 questions in 40 minutes**, 4 passages with 9 questions each. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** and one passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.** All passages and questions are original.

rows: Social Science (language and schooling, with a data table)

items: Sit somewhere quiet with no phone and no dictionary. Keep scrap paper and a pencil for your passage map.
Start the timer and do not pause it. The section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about **10 minutes per passage**: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
For the passage with a table, read the table title and column headings before the questions, and check every number you use against the right row and column.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so **answer every question**. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score.

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original memoir-style story. The narrator remembers the winter she spent living with her grandmother in Alexandria. The family is fictional.

[1] The winter I was fifteen, my parents went to work abroad for a year and sent me to live with my grandmother in Alexandria. I had visited her every summer of my life, when the city was loud with holidaymakers and the beaches were crowded with umbrellas, but I had never seen it in January. In January, I discovered, Alexandria belonged to the wind. It came off the sea in long grey pushes, rattling the shutters of her flat and throwing spray across the Corniche, so that cars drove with their wipers on under a dry sky.

[2] My grandmother was seventy-three. She had taught chemistry at a girls' school for thirty-five years, and she still spoke to me as though I were a fairly promising student who had not done the reading. On my first morning she knocked on my door at half past six. "I swim at seven," she said. "You may come and watch, or you may come and swim. You may not stay in bed feeling sorry for yourself."

[3] I chose to watch. I stood on the sand in two sweaters while she walked into the sea in a black swimming costume and a white rubber cap, with the steady, unhurried step of someone crossing a kitchen. A few others were already in the water: two old men who argued about football while they floated, and a woman of about my grandmother's age who swam up and down in straight lines, as if she were mowing a lawn. They called greetings to my grandmother, and she answered each by name. Afterwards, wrapped in a towel washed so often it was nearly transparent, she drank tea from a flask and did not ask me a single question.

[4] For two weeks I watched. I told myself it was because of the cold, which was true, and not because I was afraid, which was also true. I was afraid of a great many things that winter: of the new school where everyone already had friends, of the long telephone calls with my mother in which neither of us said what we meant, of the feeling that my life had been put on a shelf for a year while I waited to be collected.

[5] One morning the wind dropped. The sea lay flat and pale, the colour of a spoon, and my grandmother, coming out of the water, looked at me on the sand and said, "Today it is kind. It will not be kind again for a week." Then she simply waited, the way she used to wait in her classroom for a girl to answer a question she knew the girl could answer.

[6] The first shock of the water was so complete that for a moment I could not breathe at all. Then I could, in short, ragged gasps, and then, slowly, in longer ones. My grandmother swam beside me without speaking. When I said, through chattering teeth, that I was going to die, she said, "Not today," and turned onto her back to look at the sky.

[7] I lasted perhaps three minutes. On the sand, the woman who swam like a lawnmower handed me her own towel and told me I had done very well for a first time, and one of the old men declared that I had obviously inherited my grandmother's lungs. I drank the tea from the flask. It was too sweet, and it was the best thing I had ever tasted.

[8] I swam most mornings after that, except when the wind made it impossible, and by March I could stay in for ten minutes. I would like to say that the swimming solved my other fears, but it did not, not directly. The school remained difficult; the telephone calls remained awkward. What changed was smaller and harder to name. I had learned that the first minute of something cold is the worst minute, and that if you keep breathing, the second is already different.

[9] My grandmother never once told me this. She was a chemistry teacher, and she believed that some things are understood only through experiment. Years later, when I asked her why she had not pushed me into the water during those first two weeks, she looked at me with mild surprise. "You were not ready to learn," she said. "Watching was the first part of the lesson."
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?
c: A teenager describes daily life on Alexandria's crowded summer beaches.
A retired chemistry teacher explains the methods she used in her classroom.
A narrator explains how learning to swim solved all of her problems at a new school.
An adult narrator recalls how her grandmother's patient example helped her face a cold winter swim and, in a small way, her other fears.
questions.e: The story follows the narrator from watching on the sand to swimming, and paragraphs 8–9 explain the small but real change it made. The claim that swimming solved all her problems is exactly what the narrator denies in paragraph 8.
ce: Wrong season and focus: the story takes place in winter, and summer is mentioned only in passing.
Wrong narrator: the granddaughter tells the story, and the grandmother's teaching is only background.
Contradicted: paragraph 8 says the swimming did not solve her other fears directly and school "remained difficult."
Right: the passage moves from watching to swimming and ends with what the narrator learned.

c: her parents had gone to work abroad for a year.
she wanted to attend a better school in Alexandria.
her grandmother was ill and needed someone to look after her.
she had asked to spend a winter learning to swim.

questions.q: The description of the grandmother walking into the sea "with the steady, unhurried step of someone crossing a kitchen" (paragraph 3) mainly suggests that she:
c: is careless about the danger of swimming alone.
treats the cold winter sea as an ordinary part of her daily life.
wants to finish her swim as quickly as possible.
is unsure how deep the water is.
questions.e: Comparing the sea to a kitchen shows that, for her, walking into cold water is as normal as walking across her own home. "Unhurried" rules out the idea that she wants to finish quickly.
ce: Not supported: she is not alone, and nothing suggests carelessness.

Contradicted: "unhurried" means she is in no rush.

waiting for her mother's permission to swim in winter.

c: generous.
type.
polite.
calm and gentle.

c: was growing impatient with the narrator's fear.
doubted that the narrator could manage the cold water.
believed the narrator was capable and wanted the decision to be the narrator's own.
wanted to test the narrator's knowledge of chemistry.

Passage II — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about language and schooling. The researcher, the study and the figures in the table are fictional.

[1] Imagine arriving at school on your first day and discovering that your teacher speaks a language you have barely heard. For many children around the world, this is not imagination but ordinary life. In a number of countries, the language of the classroom is a national or international language, while children grow up speaking one of many local languages at home. These children are asked to do two difficult things at once: learn to read, and learn the language they are reading in.

[2] Many education researchers argue that this is the wrong order. A child who already speaks a language, they point out, has a large store of words and sentence patterns ready to use. Learning to read in that language means matching written symbols to sounds and meanings the child already knows. Learning to read in an unfamiliar language means decoding words that may carry no meaning at all. Supporters of "home-language-first" education therefore propose that children learn to read in their home language for the first few years while studying the official language as a subject, and then move gradually to the official language as the main language of teaching.

[3] Critics raise practical and social objections. Printing books in many languages is expensive, and teachers must be trained to teach reading in each one. Some parents, too, are doubtful. They know that exams, universities and many jobs use the official language, and they fear that time spent on the home language is time taken away from the language that matters most for their children's future.

[4] A study led by education researcher Nadia Mensah set out to test these competing claims. Working in one multilingual region, her team followed pupils in twenty-four rural primary schools for five years. Twelve schools taught reading in the children's home language for the first three years, adding the official language step by step; the other twelve used the official language from the first day. The schools were chosen to be as similar as possible in size, distance from the nearest town and family income. Some of the team's results appear in the table below.

Measure | Home-language-first schools | Official-language-first schools
Grade 2: pupils who could read a simple text in their home language | 71% | 18%
Grade 2: pupils who could read a simple text in the official language | 26% | 35%
Grade 5: pupils who could read a grade-level text in the official language | 62% | 47%
Grade 5: pupils who had repeated at least one school year | 9% | 17%

[5] The early results seemed to confirm the parents' fears. In Grade 2, pupils in the home-language-first schools were behind in reading the official language. But they could read, and that turned out to matter. Mensah's team found that skills learned in one language—sounding out words, following a story, guessing a meaning from context—carried over when pupils began reading in the second. By Grade 5, the home-language-first group had not only caught up but moved ahead in reading the official language, and fewer of its pupils had been held back a year.

[6] Mensah is careful about what the study can and cannot show. The schools were not chosen at random, and the home-language-first schools may have had more enthusiastic teachers, since they had volunteered for a new programme. The study also measured reading, not speaking, and it ended in Grade 5, long before the exams that worry parents most. "Our results describe one region, one set of languages and one programme," she writes. "They are encouraging, not final."

[7] Still, she argues, the findings should change how families and governments think about the choice. The question is not whether children should learn the official language; nearly everyone agrees that they should. The question is how they can learn it best. If the study's pattern holds elsewhere, a child who first learns to read in a language she understands is not losing time at all. She is building the foundation on which the second language will later stand.

A study suggests that teaching children to read first in their home language may help them read the official language better in the long run.

Printing books in many languages is too expensive for most governments.
questions.e: The passage sets out the debate, reports Mensah's results and ends by saying the findings should change how people think about the choice. Abandoning the official language is the opposite of the author's point in paragraph 7.

Right: the passage presents the debate, the study and its cautious conclusion.

Too narrow: cost is one objection in paragraph 3, not the main idea.

Passage III — Humanities

HUMANITIES: This passage is from an original essay about the mashrabiya, a traditional wooden window screen.

[1] Walk through the older streets of Cairo and look up. Above the shops and doorways, wooden boxes project from the walls of old houses, their fronts made of thousands of small turned pieces of wood fitted into delicate patterns. These are mashrabiyas, and for centuries they were among the most familiar features of houses in Cairo and many other cities of the Arab world. To a visitor they are ornaments. To the people who built them, they were machines—quiet, slow and made of wood, but machines all the same, each designed to solve several problems at once.

[2] The first problem was the sun. In a hot, bright city, an open window lets in glare and heat along with light. The lattice of a mashrabiya breaks direct sunlight into thousands of small points, so that the room behind it receives a soft, even light and much of the heat stays outside. The second problem was air. Because the screen is full of openings, it lets breezes pass even while it blocks the sun, and the room behind it can stay cooler than one with a solid shutter. According to one common explanation, the name itself comes from the Arabic word for drinking, because jars of water were placed in the screen's openings, where the moving air cooled them.

[3] The third problem was privacy. Traditional houses in Cairo were often built close together along narrow streets, and family life in them was private. The mashrabiya allowed the people inside to look out at the street—to watch a procession, to see who was knocking at the door—without being seen themselves. From outside, the screen looks dark and solid; from inside, it is a window. In many examples the lattice is finer at the height of a seated person's eyes and wider above, so that privacy is greatest where it is needed, and light and air are greatest where privacy matters less.

[4] The mashrabiya also shaped the life of the street. A house with screens on its upper floors was not closed to the city, but it was not open to it either. It took part in the street's life on its own terms. Some historians of architecture have argued that this balance between connection and protection is the key to understanding the whole traditional house, which often turned inward around a courtyard while keeping up a careful conversation with the street.

[5] In the twentieth century the mashrabiya fell out of use. Glass windows, concrete walls and, later, air conditioning made it seem old-fashioned, and the skilled craftsmen who turned and joined the wooden pieces grew fewer. Many screens were removed, and some were sold to collectors abroad, where they hung in museums or in the homes of the wealthy as decoration, cut off from the climate and the way of life they had been designed for.

[6] More recently, however, architects have returned to the idea. The Arab World Institute in Paris, completed in 1987, has a wall of metal panels whose openings, inspired by traditional lattice patterns, widen and narrow in response to light. The Al Bahar Towers in Abu Dhabi are wrapped in a screen of panels that open and close as the sun moves across the sky. Such buildings are often praised as a meeting of tradition and technology.

[7] They deserve the praise, but they also raise a question. A pattern can be copied far more easily than a purpose. Across the region, many new buildings now carry decorative screens printed onto glass or fixed in front of sealed windows, where they let in no breeze and hide no one. They look like mashrabiyas, but they do none of the work. The real lesson of the old screens is not a pattern of wooden pieces. It is a way of thinking: start with the climate and the life of the people inside, and let the form follow from both. A building that learns that lesson may look nothing like a mashrabiya and still be its true descendant.

Passage IV — Natural Science

NATURAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the chemistry of the oceans. The researcher and the experiment in paragraph 6 are fictional.

[1] Most discussions of carbon dioxide and climate focus on the air. The oceans, however, have quietly been doing a great deal of work. Since the start of the industrial era, they have absorbed roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by burning coal, oil and gas. Without this, the gas would have built up in the atmosphere even faster, and the planet would have warmed more than it has. But the oceans have not absorbed this carbon without cost. The cost is a slow change in the chemistry of seawater, known as ocean acidification.

[2] The chemistry begins simply. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, some of it reacts with the water to form carbonic acid, the same weak acid that gives fizzy drinks their slight bite. The acid releases hydrogen ions, and the more hydrogen ions water contains, the more acidic it is. Scientists measure this on the pH scale, on which lower numbers mean more acidic. The average pH of the surface ocean has fallen from about 8.2 before the industrial era to about 8.1 today.

[3] That change sounds tiny, and it is easy to misunderstand. Seawater has not become an acid; with a pH above 7, it is still slightly alkaline. "Acidification" describes the direction of the change, not the destination. And because the pH scale is logarithmic—each whole step represents a tenfold change—a fall of just 0.1 means that the concentration of hydrogen ions has risen by about 30 percent. In chemistry, as in many things, small numbers can hide large changes.

[4] The organisms most at risk are those that build shells or skeletons from calcium carbonate: corals, oysters, mussels, sea urchins and many kinds of plankton. To build, these creatures need carbonate ions from the water. But the extra hydrogen ions combine with carbonate ions, leaving fewer available for building. In more acidic water, shell-builders must spend more energy to make their shells, and under extreme conditions existing shells may begin to dissolve.

[5] Some of the clearest early warnings came not from laboratories but from businesses. In the late 2000s, oyster hatcheries on the Pacific coast of the United States suffered heavy losses of young oysters. Investigators linked the deaths to deep, carbon-rich water that winds sometimes push up toward the coast. Very young oysters, which must build their first shells within days, could not cope with it. Some hatcheries now monitor the water closely and treat it before it reaches their tanks—a solution that works for a hatchery but obviously not for an ocean.

c: argue that ocean acidification is mostly harmless.
add balance by noting uncertainties and exceptions while stressing how unusually fast the present change is.

Some seagrasses grow faster in water rich in carbon dioxide.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for **every** question, including the ones you got right, and check the reason given for each choice: make sure you chose the answer for the right reason.

List your wrong answers by category (Key Ideas and Details, Craft and Structure, Integration of Knowledge and Ideas) and by trap: too extreme, too narrow, reversed, mixed-up details, or true but not in the passage.

Weak on main ideas, details and inferences? Go back to **Main Idea and Summary Questions**, **Detail Questions: "According to the Passage"**, **Relationships: Sequence, Cause–Effect and Comparison** and **Inference Questions: "It Can Reasonably Be Inferred"**.
Weak on word meaning, purpose and tone? Review **Words and Phrases in Context**, **Purpose, Function and Text Structure** and **Point of View, Tone and Perspective**.
Weak on the table and evidence questions? Review **Passages with Charts, Tables and Graphs** and **Evaluating Arguments: Claims, Evidence and Reasoning**.
If you ran out of time, re-read **ACT Reading Strategy: Read Fast, Answer Smart** and practise one passage a day with a 10-minute timer.
